TITLE: Investigating Bidirectional Dependency Between Scene and Trajectory
PROPOSAL: We modify the one-shot trajectory predictor to a two-shot paradigm where the first shot predicts the future scene and the ego vehicle's state, and the second shot refines this prediction by considering the vehicle's potential actions and the impact on the scene.
CONTROLS: Compare with (1) a baseline one-shot trajectory predictor; (2) an ablation of the second shot; (3) a version that uses a world model to predict the future scene.

(In the future, I can propose alternative action architectures to investigate the bidirectional dependency, such as using a recurrent model to iteratively predict and refine the scene and trajectory.)

TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Future Scene Anticipation on Trajectory Planning
PROPOSAL: We design a set of experiments where we evaluate the performance of our two-shot paradigm (proposal 1) under different future time horizons and scene variability, using the KITTI dataset and the commonly used ADAS eval metric. We compare our approach with (1) a baseline planner that ignores scene anticipation and relies solely on the current state and one-shot trajectory prediction; (2) a global planner that considers the optimal trajectory but neglects scene dynamics.
CONTROLS: We will also evaluate our approach in a scenario with reduced scene variability and low time horizon to understand its minimum requirements and limitations.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see performance gains for our two-shot paradigm under high scene variability and long time horizons, but some degradation when scene variability is low. 

(In future turns, I can propose a more advanced scene anticipation component that allows our two-shot paradigm to also predict and handle obstacles and other dynamic entities.)

TITLE: Bidirectional Scenario Forecasting for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel end-to-end driving model, dubbed "BiDrive", that not only forecasts future scene dynamics but also incorporates the expected future actions of the ego vehicle and surrounding agents. BiDrive will consist of two interconnected components: a world model predicting future scene states and a planner considering the anticipated future scene and intended ego actions to generate a trajectory. We will utilize a variant of the widely used Temporal Difference learning framework, specifically, TD3 BCQ, combining temporal consistency and exploration.
CONTROLS: Compare BiDrive against two baselines: (1) a one-shot trajectory predictor using TD3 BCQ on the same dataset, and (2) a world model that predicts future scene states without considering ego actions or surrounding agents. Additionally, we will ablate the planner and world model components separately to understand their individual contributions.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours to train BiDrive on the Udacity self-driving car dataset.
PREDICTION: We expect BiDrive to outperform both baselines in terms of planning quality, particularly in complex scenarios where the future scene significantly depends on the ego vehicle's actions. Potential failure points include the difficulty in learning accurate scene dynamics and balancing exploration-exploitation trade-offs in planning.

TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Anticipated Future Actions on Planning Quality
PROPOSAL: To investigate how the anticipation of future actions by surrounding agents affects planning quality in BiDrive, we will conduct an ablation study where the planner in BiDrive is forced to disregard the expected future actions of others. We will compare the results to the original BiDrive setup, as well as a scenario where only the ego vehicle's future actions are considered. Additionally, we will experiment with different levels of observation horizon for the surrounding agents, from myopic (only current state) to fully-fledged anticipated future states.
CONTROLS: Compare three setups: BiDrive with anticipated future actions by all agents, BiDrive without anticipated future actions by others, and BiDrive with only ego vehicle's future actions considered. We will also evaluate the impact of different observation horizons for surrounding agents.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the ablated planner.
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant drop in planning quality when the planner disregards anticipated future actions by surrounding agents, especially in scenarios with complex surrounding traffic or pedestrians. The results will also provide insights on the importance of balancing ego actions and considering the impact of others.

TITLE: Comparing World Modeling Benchmarks for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
PROPOSAL: To critically evaluate the strengths and limitations of existing world modeling benchmarks for end-to-end autonomous driving, we will reproduce and compare the performance of popular world models (e.g., PredRNN++, World-RCAN, and Vision-World-RCAN) on two real-world datasets: the Udacity self-driving car dataset and the nuScenes dataset. We will utilize commonly used metrics, such as Intersection-over-Union (IoU) and mean absolute error (MAE), to evaluate the accuracy of scene predictions. Additionally, we will investigate the impact of different scene representations (e.g., RGB, semantic segmentation maps) on world model performance.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of four world models, each evaluated on two datasets and with two scene representations (RGB and semantic segmentation maps). We will also use a no-free-lunch baseline, where the models are blind to future observations and can only predict based on the current scene.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the world models on both datasets.
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the compared world models will demonstrate varying strengths and weaknesses across the two datasets, highlighting the complexity of scene prediction in autonomous driving. TITLE: Temporal Consistency and Exploration Regularization for Planning-aware World Models
PROPOSAL: To address the issue of planning-aware world models lacking a clear objective for balancing exploration and exploitation, we will introduce a novel regularization scheme that enforces temporal consistency in scene predictions while promoting exploration. This modification will be integrated into the TD3 BCQ framework used in BiDrive, allowing us to train world models that can effectively predict the evolution of the scene while exploring unseen possibilities.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the TD3 BCQ model with and without the temporal consistency and exploration regularization on a mixture of novel and unseen test scenes.
COST: Estimated 150 GPU-hours to train the modified TD3 BCQ model.
PREDICTION: We expect the temporal consistency and exploration regularization to improve planning-aware world models' performance in scenarios with high uncertainty, leading to more robust planning decisions and better adaptability in complex driving situations. If not optimized properly to the world model parameters, the expected performance could potentially stagnate.

TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Multi-Frame Planner Updates on Planning Quality
PROPOSAL: To further improve the planning quality of BiDrive, we will experiment with updating the planner with multi-frame trajectories instead of a single future frame. This will allow us to capture the evolution of the scene and the ego vehicle's position across multiple time steps, potentially leading to more informed and robust planning decisions. We will evaluate the impact of this change on planning quality, as well as compute efficiency and model training stability.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the baseline BiDrive model against variants that update the planner with 2-frame and 4-frame trajectories. We will also ablate the impact of different planning horizon lengths and scene prediction noise levels on the model's performance.
COST: Estimated 180 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the multi-frame planner variants.
PREDICTION: We expect the use of multi-frame planner updates to improve planning quality, especially in scenarios with high scene variability and dynamic traffic, but may also introduce additional computational overhead and sensitivity to hyperparameters.

TITLE: Transfer Learning for Efficient Adaption to New Driving Scenarios
PROPOSAL: To enable BiDrive to adapt efficiently to new and unseen driving scenarios, we will investigate the application of transfer learning techniques. Specifically, we will fine-tune pre-trained BiDrive models on a limited amount of data from the new scenario, allowing us to leverage the knowledge and features learned in previous domains. We will evaluate the effectiveness of transfer learning in terms of adaptation speed, planning quality, and model size efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of transfer learning approaches using different pre-trained models and fine-tuning strategies (e.g., feature-based vs. endpoint-based fine-tuning, joint learning of source and target tasks). Additionally, we will evaluate the adaptability of BiDrive on various datasets (e.g., nuScenes, Udacity, and simulated data).
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours to fine-tune BiDrive models on new scenarios and evaluate transfer learning approaches.
PREDICTION: We expect transfer learning to significantly enhance the adaptability and efficiency of BiDrive in real-world driving scenarios, reducing the need for large amounts of new training data. However, potential pitfalls include overfitting to the source domain or neglecting critical features in the target domain.

TITLE: Human-in-the-Loop Evaluation of BiDrive Planning Decisions
PROPOSAL: To assess the effectiveness and reliability of BiDrive's planning decisions in real-world driving scenarios, we will conduct human-in-the-loop evaluations using a driving simulator or a controlled environment. Human evaluators will interact with the simulated vehicle and provide feedback on the planner's decisions, allowing us to identify and quantify the challenges and limitations of BiDrive in complex and dynamic scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare the human evaluation results against the performance of BiDrive in automated and simulated settings. We will also evaluate the agreement between human evaluators and the planner's decisions, as well as the impact of different design choices (e.g., planning horizon, prediction accuracy) on human satisfaction and perception of safety.
COST: Estimated 400 person-hours to conduct human-in-the-loop evaluations, assuming 20 evaluators and 20 scenarios.
PREDICTION: We expect the human-in-the-loop evaluations to provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of BiDrive's planning decisions, helping to identify areas for improvement and fine-tune the model's performance in real-world driving scenarios.

TITLE: Lightweight Deployment of BiDrive for Edge Computing in Autonomous Vehicles
PROPOSAL: To enable the widespread adoption of BiDrive in autonomous vehicles, we will investigate optimized models, algorithms, and software frameworks for deploying BiDrive on edge computing hardware. We aim to reduce the computational requirements and memory footprint of BiDrive while maintaining its planning performance, making it suitable for real-time deployment in resource-constrained automotive systems.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of BiDrive models with varying complexity, regularization, and quantization techniques on different edge computing platforms. We will also evaluate the impact of delayed or partial knowledge updates on BiDrive's performance and adaptability.
COST: Estimated 250 person-hours to optimize and deploy BiDrive on edge computing hardware, assuming 10 variants of the model and 5 different platforms.
PREDICTION: We expect the optimized deployment of BiDrive to achieve significant reductions in computational requirements and memory footprint, enabling its real-time deployment in edge computing environments while maintaining high planning quality and adaptability.
